notes:
I've put these notes together from the sources I could reach. Searches and page loads were limited, so some verses are thin. I couldn't load anything from netbible.org's main site, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, ligonier.org, desiringgod.org, lcms.org or seedbed.com. The Catholic and Orthodox material below comes from Church Fathers as quoted in older Protestant commentaries, not from those churches' own sites. I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so that topic is left out.

Two caveats:
- The Enduring Word page cut off partway through, after verse 16. My Enduring Word notes for verses 25, 27 and 28 come from search-result excerpts of the same page.
- The Pulpit Commentary page on biblehub also cut off after verse 12.

---

**v. 1:** The section is Solomon's proverbs, gathered under Hezekiah. Guzik says Hezekiah and his men found them and added them to the Bible about 270 years after Solomon's death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
The Pulpit Commentary says the word "also" points back to an earlier collection, probably the one in Proverbs 10–22:16, nine of whose proverbs are repeated here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Its sermon notes suggest a picture of Hezekiah's scribes searching old libraries and collecting the forgotten sayings of his famous ancestor. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-25.html

**v. 2:** Pulpit: God's chief glory is his mystery, the unfathomable nature of who he is and what he does. Our limited minds cannot grasp the infinite and can only take in what God chooses to reveal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Guzik applies the second line to science. Searching out what God has hidden in creation shows part of humanity's glory, even "the glory of kings." He quotes Garrett, a modern scholar, that the verse seems to be a deliberate tribute to Solomon and Hezekiah as scholar-kings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
Matthew Henry notes that some take "concealing" to mean that God pardons sin by covering it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm
Lutheran: in the Pulpit sermon notes, Luther says that in God's kingdom we should not demand the why and wherefore but trust, while in the world's kingdom a ruler should ask why and trust nothing. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-25.html

**v. 3:** Pulpit: this verse is linked to verse 2 by the shared idea of "searching." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Guzik quotes Ross that people cannot know a king's decisions, perhaps because of his greater wisdom, his whims, or the need for secrecy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
The Pulpit sermon notes draw a lesson: don't be quick to criticise the actions of those in power, since their reasons may go deeper than we can see. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-25.html

**vv. 4–5:** Guzik: just as dross is removed from silver, wicked advisers and companions should be removed from rulers. Then their rule will be established in righteousness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
Pulpit: the king finds out the wicked and punishes them, which strengthens his rule and keeps his dynasty going. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Henry: a ruler's serious effort to suppress vice and reform his people is the surest support for his government. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm

**vv. 6–7a:** Guzik links this to Jesus' teaching in Luke 14:8–11. If we humble ourselves properly, we may be invited to a higher place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
Henry calls Jesus' parable "borrowed from this." He warns that we must not fake modesty as a trick to win honour. We should be truly humble, because God and people honour the humble. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm
Pulpit says the Hebrew word for "prince" means any nobleman. The point is to spare yourself the embarrassment of being moved out of a seat you knowingly took from someone else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm

**vv. 7b–8:** Where the verse break falls matters. Pulpit notes that the Hebrew is elliptical. Delitzsch and others read the line as a question: "lest it be said at the end, What will you do?" Jerome's Latin joins the end of verse 7 to verse 8: "What your eyes have seen, do not reveal hastily in a quarrel." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm, https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-25.html
Guzik: another reason to avoid court is that you might lose and be shamed. Many people who sue are unrealistically sure they will win. He connects this with 1 Corinthians 6:1–8 and Luke 12:57–59. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/

**vv. 9–10:** Pulpit reads the second line as "the secret of another." It means don't bring in a third party, and don't use anything someone confided in you to help your case. It also comments that the motive offered here, fear of public shame, clearly falls short of Christian morality. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Guzik quotes Kidner that running to the law or the neighbours usually means running away from dealing with the person directly (Matthew 18:15). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
Henry: try to settle things privately first, and you may find there is no need to go to law. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm

**v. 11:** Ellicott and Pulpit say the Hebrew can mean "in due season" or "upon its wheels." The best reading is a word spoken with proper thought for time and place. "Apples of gold" are golden-coloured fruit, not fruit made of gold. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/25-11.htm
Pulpit cites Canon Tristram's view that the "apple" was the apricot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Guzik quotes Trapp: it is a great skill to time a word well (Isaiah 50:4), "to set it upon the wheels." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/

**v. 12:** Pulpit: the comparison isn't stated, only implied by setting the two ideas side by side. The listening ear accepts a wise rebuke and wears it like a treasured ornament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Guzik: the fitting word may itself be a rebuke. When a wise rebuker meets a listening ear, it is like fine jewellery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/

**v. 13:** Guzik quotes Garrett: the verse doesn't mean it snows at harvest, which would be a disaster. It refers to snow brought down from the mountains to refresh workers in the harvest heat. Guzik applies it to God's people as faithful messengers of the gospel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/

**v. 14:** Pulpit: the proverb is about disappointed promises. In the East, clouds and wind usually come before heavy rain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Guzik gives Ananias and Sapphira as examples of people who want a reputation for generosity without being generous. He notes that Jude 12 uses the same picture. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/

**v. 15:** Guzik gives William Wilberforce as an example of patience winning over rulers. He quotes Bridges that a gentle tongue breaking a bone seems a paradox but shows how gentleness is stronger than harshness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
Pulpit sermon notes: patience is like a silent hammer, quietly crushing resistance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/proverbs-25.html
Henry: people say hard words break no bones, so we should bear them patiently. It seems soft words do break bones, so we should use them wisely. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm

**v. 16:** Guzik: too much of a good thing is harmful and works against you. He quotes Kidner that since Eden, people have thought something wonderful lay beyond God's "enough," when what lies there is nausea. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
The Pulpit sermon notes extend this to spiritual life: yes, you can have too much of one kind of religious food, and those who live on only one kind will suffer for it. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-25.html

**v. 17:** Pulpit: the Hebrew literally says "make your foot precious," that is, rare. The verse is loosely tied to verse 16 as a call to moderation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Guzik: a wise person notices when a neighbour may be tiring of them. Good relations with neighbours make life much better. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/

**vv. 18–19:** Pulpit: a false witness hands his neighbour weapons of death. The second line comes from the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:16). A faithless man can no more be relied on in trouble than a loose or broken tooth or a dislocated foot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Guzik links the two verses: the false witness is often also the person who fails you in trouble. In one way he causes pain; in the other he is a pain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/

**v. 20:** Pulpit: the verse gives three pictures of something wrong or out of place, building up to the third, the main point. The wording of the first line is uncertain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm
Plumptre, cited in the Pulpit sermon notes, sees the fizzing of acid poured on soda as a picture of the irritation badly timed songs cause. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-25.html
Guzik quotes Morgan: it is wrong to make merry around someone grieving. It deepens their distress instead of easing it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
Henry: trying to cheer up mourners adds to their grief, because it looks as if their friends hardly care. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm

**v. 21:** Pulpit: Paul quotes this famous saying (except the last line) from the Greek Old Testament in Romans 12:20. The old idea of hating your enemies is firmly rejected here. It cites Elisha feeding the Syrians (2 Kings 6:22). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/25.htm

**v. 22: the main verse where readings differ**
- *Mainstream (shame leading to repentance):* NET Bible note: the burning coals stand for pangs of conscience, which kindness produces more readily than violence. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=25&verse=22
  Ellicott: you will make him burn with shame at the wrong he has done you. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/25-22.htm
  Guzik (Calvary Chapel): most likely it means a burning conviction our kindness places on our enemy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
- *Baptist (Gill):* the coals are not meant to increase his punishment, but to bring him to shame and repentance for his wrongs, and God rewards you whether or not it works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/25-22.htm
- *Wesleyan/Methodist (Adam Clarke):* the coals are not to consume him but to melt him into kindness, a picture taken from smelting metal ore. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/25-22.html
- *Reformed/Puritan:* these writers allow a harder second outcome. The Geneva Study Bible says you will overcome him, as if by force, so that his own conscience makes him admit your kindness. Matthew Poole gives two readings. One is in a bad sense: your kindness worsens his sin and brings God's vengeance on him sooner. The other is in a good sense: you melt him into repentance. If the coals don't melt him, they will consume him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/25-22.htm
  Matthew Henry (labelled Nonconformist/Calvinist on StudyLight) also holds both: kindness is a likely way to win them over. If it fails, it will add to his sin and punishment and heap God's wrath on his head. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/25-22.html
- *The Cambridge Bible* (listed among biblehub's verse commentaries) reads it as simply taking the most effective revenge on him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/25-22.htm
- *Cultural background:* Constable, a teacher from the bible.org circle quoted on StudyLight, ties it to people carrying borrowed live coals home on their heads. The person repaid with good for evil feels uncomfortable even as he receives a gift, because he feels guilty for wronging his neighbour. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/25-22.html
  GotQuestions mentions a possible Egyptian ritual in which a guilty person carried a pan of burning coals on his head to show repentance. https://www.gotquestions.org/treat-our-enemies.html
- *Church Fathers (Catholic/Orthodox heritage), via Pulpit:* Chrysostom and other Fathers think God's vengeance is meant, as in Psalm 11:6 and 140:10. Pulpit itself follows Augustine, for whom the coals are a picture of the deep pain of remorse and repentance. It also quotes Francis de Sales on doing good so the coals burn up all ill will and move him to love you. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/25-22.htm, https://biblehub.com/proverbs/25-22.htm
  Sources disagree about Chrysostom. A Bible Hub article quotes his Homilies on Romans as saying "It is not to burn him up, but to melt him down." https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_heaping_burning_coals.htm

**v. 23:** The Hebrew can be read two ways. The KJV, following the Latin, has "drives away rain." In that reading the listener's angry face silences the gossip. Gill prefers this and says a stern look checks them and stops what they are doing. Barnes says the alternative reading is far more accurate: the northwest wind in Palestine usually brings rain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/25-23.htm
Coffman sets out the difference. In the KJV the angry face belongs to the person hearing the gossip. In the RSV it belongs to the victim of the slander. Constable takes the second view. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/25-23.html

**v. 24:** Henry: the verse shows how much pity is due to those badly matched with a quarrelsome spouse, and this applies to husbands as much as wives. It is better to be alone than married to someone who hinders rather than helps. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm

**v. 25:** Guzik applies it to good news of every kind, not least the gospel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
Henry: heaven is a far country, and good news from there, in the gospel and the Spirit's witness, is refreshing. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm
Pulpit admits the gospel reading is not in the text itself: we can't claim Solomon had this in mind, but the principle can still be applied to the gospel. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-25.html

**v. 26:** Henry calls it a sad thing and a public harm, like a muddied fountain or polluted spring, when the righteous fall down before the wicked. His full explanation was cut off in what I could see. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm

**v. 27:** The Hebrew is hard to read here. Ellicott: "the sense of this passage is very doubtful." Barnes thinks the text is probably damaged. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/25-27.htm, https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/proverbs/25-27.html
- *Traditional reading (seeking praise for yourself):* Poole says seeking honour and applause from people is not only sinful but shameful, a sign of a vain and petty spirit. Gill offers this reading and also the literal "searching out their glory is glory." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/25-27.htm
  Guzik: we should seek God's glory and not worry about our own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-25/
- *Scholarly emendation:* Delitzsch slightly changes the vowel points to get "but to search out hard things is an honour," a contrast between pleasure and study. Pulpit rejects this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/25-27.htm
- *Catholic reading (Vulgate, Gregory the Great):* the Douay-Rheims has "he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/proverbs/25-27.html Pulpit agrees with Pope Gregory that God's glory lifts us up when searched with moderation but crushes us when we dig beyond our powers. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/25-27.htm
  Clarke (Wesleyan) also sees a warning that whoever searches too far into mysteries is likely to be confounded by them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/25-27.html

**v. 28:** Henry: the wise person governs himself and his desires and passions, and doesn't let them rebel against reason and conscience. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_025.cfm
Guzik quotes Bridges: "the noblest conquests are gained or lost over ourselves." The first outburst of anger led to murder, and a king's careless lust led to adultery. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/proverbs/proverbs-25.cfm
Pulpit: self-control is a wall that protects the soul from temptation. When it is gone, the soul has no shelter. The Greek and Latin versions differ. The Septuagint compares the broken city to a man who acts without counsel. Jerome adds "in speaking," applying the verse to lack of restraint in speech. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-25.html
